title: Keep score: name, change, trace and debug

prompts: Without the worked example, explain: Distinguish a variable's name, current value and an instruction that changes its value.
Without the worked example, explain: Trace ordered scoring instructions, distinguishing replacement from adding to the current value.

pedagogy.rationale: Model a named store with cards, then build and trace scoring procedures. Test predictions against a partner's trace, repair initialization errors and transfer the procedure to a different game.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Read whole numbers to twenty, with oral support if needed.
Add small whole numbers and follow ordered instructions.

misconceptions.description: The variable's name is changed whenever its number changes.
misconceptions.response: Keep the name score fixed and replace the number stored beneath it.

misconceptions.description: Set score to a number is treated as adding that number.
misconceptions.response: Set replaces the current value. Add uses the current value to calculate the next one.

misconceptions.description: Initialization is repeated before every event, discarding the accumulated score.
misconceptions.response: Initialize at new-game start and retain the updated value between events.

misconceptions.description: A set instruction is ignored and the previous value is retained.
misconceptions.response: Follow every instruction in order. Set replaces the old value even if no points were earned.

misconceptions.description: A new game starts without initialization and inherits an earlier game's score.
misconceptions.response: Give each new game its stated starting value before processing events.

scenes.title: Predict before playing
scenes.learnerAction: Write a prediction and explain what must be remembered between the two turns.

content.body: Our class invents a paper target game. Each hit earns two points. A scorekeeper must remember the total between turns. Start at zero. Predict the score after two hits before moving counters. This game is an invented teaching example.

prompts.prompt: Predict the score after two hits. Explain what the scorekeeper must remember between turns.

scenes.title: A name stays; its value changes
scenes.learnerAction: Make a name card and a separate number card. Sort the examples, then explain their different jobs.

content.body: Write score above a space on paper. Put a number card beneath it. The name identifies the store. Its current value is the number there now. An instruction tells the scorekeeper what to do. After a hit, change the number card; keep the name.

blocks.prompt: Sort the name, the number and the instruction.

cards.why: This label names the store, regardless of its current number.
This number can be stored under the name score.
This tells the scorekeeper how to change the stored number.
This replaces the stored number with 1; it is not another name.

scenes.title: Trace one instruction at a time
scenes.learnerAction: Copy a three-column table: instruction, value before, value after. Move the number card after each instruction.

content.body: A trace records each instruction and its result. Set score to 0 gives 0. Add 2 gives 2; add 2 again gives 4. Set score to 1 replaces 4 with 1. Add 2 now gives 3. Setting and adding do different jobs. Order matters because each instruction uses the current state.

hints: Keep score as the label in every row.
For set, replace the old number. For add, start with the current number.

accessibility.textAlternative: A trace records each instruction and its result. Set score to 0 gives 0. Add 2 gives 2; add 2 again gives 4. Set score to 1 replaces 4 with 1. Add 2 now gives 3. Setting and adding do different jobs. Order matters because each instruction uses the current state. How does each instruction change score? Step 1: New game: set score to 0. There is no earlier game value to reuse. Step 2: Add 2: 0 becomes 2. Add 2 again: 2 becomes 4. Step 3: Set score to 1: 4 becomes 1, rather than 5. Step 4: Add 2: 1 becomes 3. The variable is still named score.

scenes.title: Build a trace with help
scenes.learnerAction: Build the instruction cards, trace them and check both decisions.

content.body: Use a new game that starts with one point. A hit adds three points. Follow two hits, then a card saying set score to 2. Record every new value. Point to the current number before following each instruction. Explain whether the last instruction adds or replaces.

hints: After each hit, add three to the number currently under score.
The final card says set to 2. It replaces the old number with 2.

Options: It stays score.; It becomes four.; It needs both score and four as names.. After the two hits, set score to 2. What is its new value? Options: 7; 2; 9.

items.prompt: The value changes from 1 to 4. What happens to the variable name?

options.feedback: The name identifies the same store while its content changes.
Four is the new value, not a new name for the store.

options.text: It needs both score and four as names.
options.feedback: One name can hold different values over time.

items.prompt: After the two hits, set score to 2. What is its new value?

options.feedback: Seven was the value before the set instruction. The instruction changes it.
Set to 2 replaces the current value with 2.
Nine comes from adding 2 to 7. The instruction says set, not add.

scenes.title: Decide when to initialize
scenes.learnerAction: Choose where initialization belongs, then use the cards to explain two hits in one game.

content.body: Initialization gives a variable its starting value. Place a new-game card before the event cards. Keep the score between turns. A new game needs a fresh start, even when the previous game ended with a score. Ask a partner to follow your cards literally.

hints: Ask whether another turn is a new game.
Reset once when a new game begins; use the retained score for later turns.

accessibility.textAlternative: Initialization gives a variable its starting value. Place a new-game card before the event cards. Keep the score between turns. A new game needs a fresh start, even when the previous game ended with a score. Ask a partner to follow your cards literally. Where should set score to 0 go? Options: Never, even when another game starts.; Once at the start of each new game.; Before every hit..

items.prompt: Where should set score to 0 go?

options.text: Never, even when another game starts.
options.feedback: Without initialization, an old game's score can carry into a new game.

options.text: Once at the start of each new game.
options.feedback: This creates a fresh game while retaining points between its turns.
That erases earlier points, so two hits can look like one hit.

scenes.title: Build and trace a fresh game
scenes.learnerAction: Create the cards and complete your own trace without the worked example.

content.body: Work independently. A new game starts at two points. A hit adds three points. A reset event sets score to one. Follow hit, hit, reset, hit. Write the starting value and a row for each event. Explain what one row tells another scorekeeper.

prompts.prompt: Record the initial value and every later value for hit, hit, reset, hit. Explain the reset row and keep the variable name visible.

scenes.title: Choose tests that could expose a mistake
scenes.learnerAction: Record three predictions, run the cards and explain any difference. Add one test of your own.

content.body: Test your procedure with no events, one hit and a hit after a reset. Predict each result before your partner follows the cards. Start each separate test as a new game. Compare predictions with the trace. A match is evidence for that case, not proof that every possible case works.

prompts.prompt: For each test, show the event sequence, predicted value and observed trace. Add a different test and explain what mistake it could reveal.

scenes.title: Repair the procedure, then retest
scenes.learnerAction: Diagnose the bug, change the cards and explain the retest results.

content.body: A fictional scorekeeper resets the score before every hit. Two hits still produce only two points. A bug is a mistake in instructions or their order. Identify the instruction that loses information. Repair the procedure, then test it with three hits and with a separate new game.

prompts.prompt: Show the repaired cards and traces for three hits and a separate new game. Explain why changing the points per hit would not fix the reset bug.

blocks.problem: A new game starts at zero; each hit should add two points.

attempt.name: A fictional scorekeeper
steps: Before each hit: set score to 0.
After each hit: add 2 to score.

blocks.question: Which repair preserves earlier points?

options.text: Move set score to 0 to the new-game start, before all turns.
options.feedback: Now later hits use the retained score. Retest three hits and a new game.

options.text: Rename score to total after every hit.
options.feedback: Renaming does not stop the reset instruction from erasing previous points.

options.text: Keep resetting but add 4 after each hit.
options.feedback: That can match two hits by accident, but each later hit still loses prior state.

correction: Initialize once at new-game start, then update the retained score for each event.

scenes.title: Make a game someone else can follow
scenes.learnerAction: Build, exchange, test and revise your procedure. Compare two event orders.

content.body: Invent a target game for classmates using paper tokens. Choose a starting score, an increase and an event that replaces the score. Write precise instructions. Ask a partner to follow them without extra explanations. Use their trace to find an unclear instruction or justify why a test matched.

prompts.prompt: Present your game cards and two traces with a changed event order. Explain one revision or a test-based reason for keeping an instruction. What stayed the same when the variable's value changed?
